To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the DID estimator and the FE estimator are less biased and yield lower standard errors than other regression‐ based estimators when there is heterogeneous response bias and time‐invariant unobservables.
the DID and FEs estimations are less biased and yield smaller standard errors in the TT than other regression‐ based estimators, especially when there is no intertemporal dependence.
the relative performance of regression estimators is sensitive to the relative importance of each source of selection on unobservable.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding how well different regression methods work in terms of minimizing selection bias on unobservables, which is the main source of selection bias in most evaluations.
understanding which regression‐based estimator is best suited for which policy context.
accounting for multiple sources of selection bias in program evaluations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the FEs estimator is the most robust estimator for estimating the TT in the absence of an RCT.
the DID and FEs estimations are less biased and are less sensitive to the magnitude of pure selection bias.
the DID and FE estimators are less sensitive to the sources of pure selection biases than the other regression‐based models.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
DID using equidistant time periods and FEs estimations are less biased and more efficient than other regression‐ based estimators in estimating the TT, but they are not immune to pure selection bias.
DID using equidistant periods and FE estimators are less affected by pure selection bias than other regression‐basis estimators.
DID using equidistant windows and FEs estimations perform better than other regression‐ based estimators in estimating the TT in the presence of pure selection bias.
The main takeaway from our work is that
researchers should be careful in choosing a regression‐based estimator to minimize pure selection bias.
researchers should be cognizant of the relative magnitude of the different sources of pure selection on unobservability in the policy context of the evaluation.
researchers need to understand the relative magnitude of different sources of pure selection biases in their data context before choosing an estimator.
